summary: In Dhul Qadah of the seventh year AH, the Prophet ﷺ fulfilled the terms of the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah by performing a make-up Umrah with approximately 2,000 companions. The Quraysh vacated Makkah for three days as agreed, and the Muslims performed tawaf, sa'y, and returned peacefully — demonstrating that Islam was now a force the Quraysh could not ignore.
narrative:
When the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah was signed in 6 AH, one of its key provisions was that the Muslims who had been turned back from Umrah that year could return the following year. They would be permitted to enter Makkah, stay for three days, perform their rites, and depart peacefully. The Quraysh would withdraw from the city for the duration of their visit.

In Dhul Qadah of 7 AH — one full lunar year after Hudaybiyyah — the Prophet ﷺ set out with approximately 2,000 companions for Makkah. Ibn Hisham records that, in keeping with the treaty terms permitting only sheathed swords as a defensive precaution, the Muslims entered the Haram with their weapons secured. The Prophet ﷺ rode his camel al-Qaswa and performed tawaf of the Kaabah while mounted, using his staff to touch the Black Stone.

Al-Tabari notes that Bilal ibn Rabah ؓ called the adhan from atop the Kaabah during this visit — a sound that moved many Makkans watching from the surrounding hills. The Quraysh had retreated to the heights of Abu Qubays and the surrounding mountains as agreed, watching from a distance as the Muslims circled the House they had built.

Ibn Hisham records a poignant detail: as the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims performed tawaf, they moved with purposeful energy — they jogged (raml) for the first three circuits and walked normally for the remaining four. This practice was reportedly instituted at the Prophet's ﷺ instruction to show the Makkans observing from the hills that the Muslims were vigorous and strong, having been told by some that the fever of Madinah had weakened them.

During the three-day stay, a notable event took place: Maymunah bint al-Harith, who had been introduced to the Prophet ﷺ by Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib, accepted a proposal of marriage. The Prophet ﷺ intended to celebrate the wedding in Makkah, but the Quraysh messengers came to remind him that the three days had elapsed and he must leave. He departed honourably, and the marriage was consummated at a place called Sarif, several kilometres outside Makkah. Maymunah ؓ became the last of the Prophet's wives and one of the Mothers of the Believers.

Ibn Kathir notes in al-Bidayah wal-Nihayah that the Umrat al-Qada was also the occasion of the conversion of Khalid ibn al-Walid and Amr ibn al-As ؓ, who had been among the fiercest opponents of Islam. Khalid ؓ, having grown disenchanted with the Quraysh leadership after Hudaybiyyah, embraced Islam just before or around this visit. His conversion brought one of Arabia's greatest military minds into the Muslim ranks. Amr ibn al-As ؓ similarly came to Islam at this time. Both would go on to be among the most consequential commanders of the early Islamic conquests.

The Umrat al-Qada demonstrated the practical power of the treaty and showed the broader Arabian world that the Muslims could travel peacefully to the most sacred site in Arabia — and that the Quraysh, for all their pride, had yielded ground. It was a significant moment in the shift of moral authority from Makkah to the new community centred in Madinah.
